extracted.intended_audience: technology transfer office staff and university/academic inventors/authors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, searching, registering, maintaining, licensing, assigning, and policing trademarks and service marks in the context of academic technology transfer and university-owned marks. Emphasizes pre-adoption searching, federal vs. state registration differences, statutory definitions, infringement/likelihood-of-confusion factors, maintenance obligations, and compliance best practices for transfers and licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-adoption investigation / comprehensive searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the mark is selected, but prior to its use, a thorough search should be undertaken to determine whether the mark is available for both use and federal registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search USPTO records (online database, office records), Trademarkscan (File 226 and File 116 for brand names), private search firms (Thompson & Thompson, Dialog, Questel/Orbit, Micropatent, Corsearch) and non-federal sources such as phone directories, yellow pages, industrial directories, and state trademark registers. The searches should cover pending application records and existing registrations to identify identical or confusingly similar marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search foreign trademark records when foreign use contemplated
rubrics_metrics.description: If use of the mark is contemplated in any foreign countries, the trademark and service mark records of those countries should also be searched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Trademarkscan database File numbers for specific countries (examples given: Canada File 127, France File 657, Germany File 672, United Kingdom File 126). Include foreign registries in pre-adoption clearance where international use or filing is planned.

rubrics_metrics.name: State trademark records searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Search the trademark and service mark records of the various states as part of availability clearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademarkscan can be utilized for state records (File 246). State records may reveal common-law or registered uses that could affect availability even if federal records are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and domain-name searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Internet to determine whether a proposed mark is being used in domain names or on websites and to search business names across the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools cited include Network Solutions (WOSIT), direct browser searches for conflicting websites, and business directories such as Big Book, Switchboard, GTE Superpages, World Pages, ZIP2. Include domain-name ownership checks when selecting a mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common misconceptions about trademark rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of frequent misunderstandings that can mislead prospective mark users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misconceptions listed: incorporation, qualification to do business, or assumed-name/state registration does not automatically create the right to use the name as a mark; one does not have an absolute right to use one's personal name as a trademark/service mark; state registration does not necessarily mean it is permissible to use the mark everywhere; an abandoned application or expired registration may still be accompanied by ongoing use and protectable common-law rights against subsequent users. Treat these as caveats during clearance and adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights based on use; first-to-use/intent-to-use rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights in a mark are based upon use, not registration; generally the first to use a mark or file an intent-to-use application in the USPTO for particular products/services is the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although registration is not required to establish rights, filing (especially an intent-to-use application) is recommended because it can provide constructive priority nationwide. Be mindful of earlier users and earlier-filed applications including foreign priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'use in commerce' (15 U.S.C. §1127)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trademark Act defines 'use in commerce' for goods and services: (1) on goods when placed on goods/containers/displays/tags/labels or associated documents and the goods are sold or transported in commerce; (2) on services when used or displayed in sale/advertising of services and the services are rendered in commerce or in more than one state or in the U.S. and a foreign country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting statutory criteria clarifies when an intent-to-use application must be converted to an actual-use basis before registration. If the nature of the goods makes placement impracticable, associated documents may satisfy the goods-use requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of federal registration on the Principal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration confers significant nationwide benefits even if actual use is geographically limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits enumerated: ability to prevent registration of identical/confusingly similar marks; availability of injunctive relief and damages in federal court; registration is prima facie evidence of validity, ownership, and exclusive rights in commerce; potential incontestability after five years' use; elimination of innocent adoption defense for users post-registration; ability to record with U.S. Customs to prevent importation of infringing/counterfeit goods. Use these benefits to justify seeking federal registration when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent-to-use versus actual-use applications (dual-application system)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO permits filing based on bona fide intent to use as well as on actual use. An applicant filing on intent-to-use must later make actual use before registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an intent-to-use application provides constructive use priority while the application is pending, giving prior rights nationwide subject to exceptions for prior users or earlier filers. Plan timing of use and filing to preserve priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term and maintenance of federal registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal registrations are valid for ten years and renewable for additional ten-year periods so long as the mark remains in actual use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between the fifth and sixth year after registration the registrant must file a declaration/affidavit of continued use; an affidavit of use must also be filed in the year prior to the end of each registration term. Failure to file required statements will cause cancellation of the registration. Track maintenance deadlines carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: State registrations are territorially limited
rubrics_metrics.description: A state registration does not confer the same nationwide rights as a federal registration; it is enforceable only within that state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually unnecessary to seek a state registration if the mark is federally registrable; obtain a state registration only if the mark cannot be federally registered or if there is a specific state-level need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood-of-confusion test (factors for infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark infringement is assessed by considering multiple factors to determine likelihood of confusion between marks, not strict identity of mark or goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors listed include: strength/weakness of plaintiff's mark; similarity of marks in sound/appearance/meaning (with examples); similarity of products or services; likelihood that prior owner will 'bridge the gap' to related goods/services; presence/absence of actual confusion (strongest evidence); defendant's good faith in adopting the mark; sophistication of potential purchasers; channels of trade; similarity of advertising media. Apply these factors holistically in enforcement/clearance decisions and litigation risk assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care and feeding of marks (avoid genericide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper use and policing of marks is essential to preserve distinctiveness and avoid genericide or dilution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines: always use the mark as a proper adjective modifying a noun (e.g., Cabbage Patch Kids dolls); never use the mark in possessive form, plural, or as a verb; avoid prefixes, suffixes, additions, or deletions; typographically distinguish the mark in text (distinctive typeface, quotation marks, all caps, or at least initial capitalization of each word); use ® for registered marks or the phrase 'Registered in the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office' and use TM/SM (or an asterisk with a legend) for unregistered marks. Include quality control and consistent usage policies internally and with licensees. (Cite: Coca-Cola ditty as a memorable reminder.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing: written agreements and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow third-party use of your mark without a written license agreement that preserves the owner's control over the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a minimum, license agreements must provide the owner the ability to monitor and control the nature and quality of the goods/services associated with the mark to avoid a 'naked license' that could dilute distinctiveness. Include provisions requiring licensee notification of potential infringing marks so the owner can police its mark. Ensure licensing preserves enforcement rights and goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments must include goodwill and be in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a mark, whether registered or not, must be in writing and must include 'the good will of the business associated with the mark' or the assignment is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment without accompanying goodwill is an 'assignment in gross' and is invalid because a mark symbolizes goodwill/reputation. Note that an intent-to-use application cannot be assigned because there is nothing to assign until the mark is in actual use. Draft assignments to transfer goodwill and associated business elements where appropriate.
